title: Device behind each log line
prompt: The IoT team wants to see the device behind each log line, when there is one. Write `solve(application_logs)` so every line shows whether it names a device, and which device and firmware.
rules: `has_device` is true when `attributes` has the key `device_id`, even if its value is missing, and false when it doesn't. It is missing when the line has no map at all.
`device_id` and `firmware` are the values under those keys, missing when the key isn't there. Keys match exactly, so `Device_ID` is a different key.
Return `log_id`, `service`, `has_device`, `device_id` and `firmware`, one row per log line.
hints: `F.map_contains_key(col, key)` checks for a key without reading its value.
Read a value by key with `F.col("attributes")["device_id"]` or `.getItem("device_id")`; a missing key gives a missing value, not an error.
Give each column its name with `alias`.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(application_logs):
    # Return log_id, service, has_device, device_id and firmware.
    return application_logs
explanation: Check the key and read the two values: `F.map_contains_key("attributes", "device_id").alias("has_device")`, `F.col("attributes")["device_id"].alias("device_id")` and `F.col("attributes")["firmware"].alias("firmware")`. `map_contains_key` looks at the keys only, so a key stored with no value still counts, and a line with no map gives a missing answer rather than false. Reading a key that isn't there gives a missing value with no error. Searching `F.map_values` for the text `device_id` looks in the wrong place: the name is a key, not a value.
